text:
The Miami-based AI startup Subquadratic came out of stealth mode last month with a huge claim. It announced that it had solved a mathematical bottleneck that had been holding back large language models for almost a decade.

The details were thin, and many people were unconvinced. But Subquadratic has started to bring the receipts, sharing the results of an independent evaluation of its new tech. The results suggest that the company’s claims might be worth paying attention to.

According to Subquadratic, it has developed a new kind of LLM, called SubQ, that is faster and cheaper and uses a lot less energy than any other model on the market. The company also claims that SubQ is able to process up to 12 times as much text at once as most other models, allowing it to carry out a range of data-heavy tasks, such as analyzing hundreds of documents or entire code bases.

What’s more, Subquadratic says, SubQ does this while more or less matching the performance of the best models put out by Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic on key tasks like coding.

The problem was that the company at first provided little evidence for its claims beyond a handful of self-published test scores. And it has yet to make SubQ widely available for people to try out themselves.

So it’s no surprise that Subquadratic’s claims were met with skepticism. Dan McAteer, an artificial-intelligence engineer, captured the overall response on X: “SubQ is either the biggest breakthrough since the Transformer … or it’s AI Theranos.”

A month on, the company has published more information about its model, including the results of additional independent tests run by the third-party firm Appen.

“We expected healthy skepticism,” says Subquadratic cofounder and chief technology officer Alex Whedon. “In hindsight, releasing the third-party benchmarks alongside the initial announcement would have preempted much of the skepticism, which is why we’re taking the time to make sure any future results are fully verified before putting them out.”

Subquadratic asked Appen, which evaluates other companies’ models, to run its tests on SubQ. The results seem to back up a lot of Subquadratic’s claims. “That was really exciting to me, it validated their architecture,” says Jeanine Sinanan-Singh, Appen’s director of generative AI research.

“I was like, ‘Wow, this could be a game changer,’ because models struggle with speed and inefficiency,” she adds. “But when you have kind of shocking results, it’s really not as credible when you say it yourself.”

SubQ won’t replace existing top models across the board, but it could offer huge increases in speed at a fraction of the typical cost for certain tasks. Subquadratic insists that in the long run, though, its breakthrough could change how LLMs are built. “We hope we’re kicking off a new age of efficiency,” says Justin Dangel, the firm’s cofounder and CEO. “We don’t think anybody will be building on transformers in a few years.”

Attention!

To understand why Subquadratic’s claims are a big deal, let’s dig into how most LLMs work. The key mechanism inside an LLM is a type of neural network called a transformer, which runs a process known as dense attention. Today’s LLMs typically chain together multiple transformers. (The foundational paper of the LLM era, published by researchers at Google in 2017, was titled “Attention Is All You Need.”)

Dense attention works like this: When a transformer processes a chunk of text, it first encodes each word (or part of a word, known as a token) with a number. To capture the meaning of the full text, it then multiplies each of those numbers with every other number for that text. For example, a piece of text 10,000 words long would kick off almost 50 million individual multiplications. That’s a lot of computation and the main reason that LLMs are notorious power hogs.

“If you want to summarize The Great Gatsby, you have to look at the first word and the last word together, and then you have to look at every other combination,” says Dangel.

As the length of the text increases, the number of computations skyrockets. That’s because each additional number must be multiplied by all other previous numbers. Double the number of words, and you roughly quadruple the number of computations, a rate of increase known as a quadratic expansion.

(You can picture this yourself: Draw a circle and mark dots around its edge. Each dot is a token. Then draw lines between pairs of dots to represent the multiplication of those two tokens. A circle with five dots will have 10 lines crossing it. Make it 10 dots and you will have 45 lines, 20 dots and you will have 190 lines, and so on.)

Slashing costs

Subquadratic’s solution is to ditch dense attention, the core operation of a transformer, in favor of what’s known as sparse attention, which slashes the number of computations needed. Instead of multiplying the number assigned to each token by every other number, sparse attention selects just some of the numbers to multiply. The idea is that not all relationships between words in a piece of text matter.

“Sparse attention says not all of those relationships are important, because they’re not,” says Whedon. “If you’re reading a book, you’re not going to look at the first and second words, first and third—that’s insane.”

It’s a simple approach, and Subquadratic is not the first to try it. “Pretty much everything under the sun has been attempted,” says Will Depue, an independent AI researcher who previously worked at OpenAI. “It’s not impossible, but it’s akin to running a four-minute mile.”

Previous techniques for selecting which numbers to multiply and which to ignore have not produced a mechanism that can capture the meaning of a document as well as dense attention can.

Subquadratic claims to have cracked the problem at last. It pitches SubQ as the first sparse-attention LLM that rivals mainstream dense-attention models in performance.

“Historically, most mechanisms have used fixed patterns, like always comparing the first word to the fifth,” says Whedon. “That’s pretty limiting. Language is too sophisticated for that. And so, one of the things that makes our mechanism unique is that we dynamically select which ones are important.”

The firm won’t say exactly how SubQ chooses which words to focus on, but the selection is calculated on the fly and differs for each piece of text the model is given. “That’s kind of where the secret sauce is,” says Whedon.

Testing, testing

The upshot is that for certain tasks, SubQ may be faster and cheaper to run than most other models. Appen evaluated SubQ on a handful of standard tests. In a straight-up speed test, which sets a baseline for how fast a model can operate in theory rather than assessing what a model can actually do, Appen found that SubQ was 56 times faster than models using FlashAttention, a previous sparse-attention technique. 

On LiveCodeBench, a test that looks at how well models perform on competitive coding problems taken from real contests, SubQ scored 89.7%, putting it in the same ballpark as other top coding models. “This model continues to provide frontier-level performance in coding,” says Appen’s Sinanan-Singh.

Subquadratic’s claims about cost are harder to verify because SubQ is not yet widely available. According to Dangel, it costs $2,600 to run Anthropic’s LLM Opus 4.6 through RULER 128, a test developed by Nvidia to assess a model’s ability to retrieve information from large data sets. And SubQ? “It cost us eight dollars,” he says.

SubQ does seem to be able to handle a lot of text at once. The model has a context window (roughly akin to a working memory) up to 12 million tokens long. Most top models today have context windows one million tokens long. In a demo that Whedon ran for me, he asked SubQ to perform a task that required it to reason about information contained in 400 documents. It responded in seconds. When he gave Perplexity—a popular LLM-powered search engine—the same task, it failed to load all 400 documents. 

Appen put SubQ through the Needle-in-a-Haystack test, which, like RULER, assesses how well a model retrieves specific information buried in a large data set. In its report, Appen states that Subquadratic’s model scored 98% with context windows six million and 12 million tokens long, “sustaining near-perfect long-context retrieval at scales few models are tested at.”

Too good to be true?

Despite the high scores, benchmarks paint an incomplete picture of what a model can and cannot do. Testing under very specific conditions is not a substitute for running a model on a wide range of real tasks.

Subquadratic is offering SubQ as a model tailored to coding and to searching very large data sets. It says that tens of thousands of potential users have already signed up for early access, including more than 500 enterprise customers. But there’s a long waitlist, and the firm has given very few people access so far. Subquadratic’s response is that it is a new, small company with limited resources and cannot serve too many people at once.

Until more people get their hands on the model and try it out for themselves, some skepticism is justified. One nagging issue is that Subquadratic reused the weights (values set within a model during training that determine how it will behave) from a version of the Chinese open-source model Qwen to bootstrap SubQ, rather than training it from scratch. That’s a common approach for model makers to take, but it cuts across Subquadratic’s claim that it has fully reinvented how LLMs work.  

“They may have built something real and useful,” says Depue. “But the public evidence does not yet justify the stronger claim that they have solved the quadratic attention bottleneck.”

In the meantime, Subquadratic cofounder Whedon insists that making something different was his only option. If you want to build a competitive model, you have to have new ideas, he says: “We’re more up against it than OpenAI is.”

text:
🤰🏻🤰🏽🤰🏿 Pregnancy Days 267 to 273 (Week 39): Phase Three: Full Term
📚 Source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. General pregnancy education only, not medical advice. Always talk with your doctor or midwife.
🔊 Your baby reaches full term this week. Every organ is formed, the reflexes are ready, and your baby already knows your voice. Which song will you sing first, and how have lullabies, nursery rhymes, and phonic songs been preparing that moment? Read on.

🗓️ Week 39 at a Glance
  Week 39 is pregnancy days 267 to 273, counted from the first day of your last period, the same way your doctor, midwife, and pregnancy calculator count. If conception happened around day 14, your baby is between 253 and 259 days old. In longer or shorter cycles, these days shift a little.
This is the week of full term. Your baby is ready to live outside the womb. The brain and lungs keep maturing up to birth. Fat makes up a bigger part of your baby's weight, helping with warmth and energy. The fingernails may reach past the fingertips.
  Your baby is about 20 inches from head to heel and weighs about 7 1/4 pounds, about the size of a small pumpkin. Your due date is next week, but your baby may come any day.

🗓️ The Week, Day by Day
  Here is the week counted in days after conception. In a 28-day cycle, add 14 to find your pregnancy day. Your baby will choose the day, so treat this as a guide.
Days 253 and 254 (pregnancy days 267 and 268): Your baby reaches full term.
Days 255 and 256 (days 269 and 270): The lungs keep making surfactant, and the brain keeps adding connections.
Day 257 (day 271): Fat keeps building, giving your baby round cheeks and soft creases.
Day 258 (day 272): The fingernails may reach past the tips of the fingers.
Day 259 (day 273): Your baby weighs about 7 1/4 pounds and is about 20 inches from head to heel.

🎉 Full Term
  Doctors call babies born from 39 weeks through 40 weeks and 6 days full term. Babies born in this window generally have the best health outcomes, with the fewest problems with breathing, feeding, and staying warm.
  Your baby is ready. Every organ is formed and working. The lungs are prepared for the first breath. The brain is ready to learn. The reflexes for sucking, swallowing, and gripping are strong.
But being ready does not mean labor will start today. Many first-time mothers give birth after their due date. Your baby will come in God's time.

🗣️ What Your Baby Knows
Your baby will not understand a single word at birth. But your baby is not a stranger to your home. Your baby knows the sound of your voice. Your baby has heard Dad's voice, the voices of brothers and sisters, and the songs your family sang every week.
  Studies show newborns pay special attention to their mother's voice and to sounds they heard often before birth. The GLAL method teaches more than that too. From conception, your baby has received your songs spirit to spirit. Now the spirit, the ears, and the voice of home will meet face to face.

🫶 Teaching Begins at Home
  From the first day, your home is your child's first school. God told His people to teach their children in the house, on the road, when lying down, and when rising up.
Your baby will learn by being held, by hearing your voice, by watching your face, and by hearing the same songs and words again and again. This is God's Home Schooling. You do not need a classroom. You need love, time, and the habits you have already built.
“And you shall explain them to your sons. And you shall meditate upon them sitting in your house, and walking on a journey, when lying down and when rising up.” (Deuteronomy 6:7, CPDV)
“Gregory Peck was born April 5, 1916. In the 1962 film To Kill a Mockingbird he played a gentle father who taught his children honesty and kindness at home, a role he called one of his favorites.”

🏥 If Labor Does Not Start
  Most women go into labor on their own between 37 and 42 weeks. If labor does not start, your doctor will talk with you about the next steps.
  Some doctors offer an induction at 39 weeks for healthy pregnancies, after talking it through with you. Others wait longer, often until 41 weeks, with extra checks of your baby. If there is a medical reason, such as high blood pressure, your doctor may recommend an earlier induction.
An induction means using medicine or other methods to help labor begin. Ask your doctor what they recommend for you and why, what methods they use, and how long it may take. Write the answers in your journal.
“I know it at first light; great is your faithfulness.” (Lamentations 3:23, CPDV)
“Lou Gehrig was born June 19, 1903. He showed up and played in 2,130 baseball games in a row, faithful day after day, and he was remembered as a gentle and humble man.”

📝 Phase Three: Sing the Whole List
For 20 weeks, Phase Three has helped you join sounds into words. Look at your Word List now. You have family words, food words, face words, sound words, praise words, light words, action words, rhymes, direction words, sense words, number words, lullaby words, thank-you words, welcome words, comfort words, and Bible names.
  This week, sing through the whole list. Take one group each day. Sing every word on the melody of the weekly song, clap the beats, and remember the week you added it.
Then circle the words you will sing first after birth. Perhaps "Hello," "Mama," "Dada," "I love you," and your baby's name. This list will become your baby's first reading list. One day, your child will see these words in print and read the very words you sang before birth. That is God's plan: sounds first, then words, then reading.
  Every word on your list is a phonic song. Together they make your family's own collection of lullabies, nursery rhymes, baby music, and kids music, built one sound at a time.
  “Write the vision and explain it on tablets.” (Habakkuk 2:2, CPDV)
  “William Howard Taft was born September 15, 1857. After serving as president of the United States, he became chief justice of the Supreme Court, the only person ever to hold both offices.”

🤰 Your Body at Thirty-Nine Weeks
  Your body is ready for birth. Your cervix may be softening and starting to thin. You may feel a lot of pressure low in the pelvis, more frequent tightenings, a low backache, and sometimes loose stools or nausea as labor gets close.
Rest as much as you can, and eat and drink to keep your strength up. Walking can feel good if your doctor says it is safe.
If you have tightenings, time them from the start of one to the start of the next. Follow your doctor's instructions for when to call and when to come in.

🏥 Arriving at the Hospital
  When you arrive in labor, a nurse will usually check you in a triage area. They will check your blood pressure, your baby's heartbeat, and your tightenings, and may check your cervix to see how far labor has gone. If labor is still early, you may be sent home to rest for a while.
There are many ways to cope with labor pain: slow breathing, changing positions, walking, a warm shower or bath, massage, music, prayer, and medicines including an epidural. Talk with your doctor ahead of time about your options, and stay open. What helps can change as labor goes on.
Bring your headphones and the weekly songs. Familiar music can help you stay calm between tightenings.

👂 Newborn Checks Before Going Home
  Before you leave the hospital, your baby will usually have several checks. A few drops of blood from the heel are tested for rare but serious conditions. A small sensor on the hand and foot checks oxygen levels to screen for some heart problems. And your baby's hearing is screened with a quick, painless test while your baby sleeps.
The hearing screen is a fitting last check for a baby who has heard your songs for months. If your baby does not pass the first screen, do not panic. It is common for a newborn to need a repeat test, often because of fluid still in the ears. Make sure any follow-up test is done.

🔧 How Labor Can Be Started
  If your doctor recommends an induction, there are several ways it can be done. A membrane sweep is when the doctor gently separates the bag of waters from the cervix during an exam, which may help labor start. Medicines placed near the cervix or taken by mouth can help soften and open it. A small balloon may be placed in the cervix to help it open.
Once the cervix is ready, your doctor may give a medicine called oxytocin through an IV to bring on tightenings, and may break your water. Induction can take hours or even a day or more, especially with a first baby. Pack extra patience, snacks for Dad, and your weekly songs.

🧭 The Stages of Labor
  Labor usually happens in stages. In early labor, the cervix slowly softens and opens, and tightenings start mild and irregular, then become more regular. This stage can last many hours. In active labor, tightenings get stronger and closer together, and the cervix opens more quickly.
In the second stage, the cervix is fully open, and you push to help your baby be born. In the third stage, after your baby is born, the placenta comes out, usually within about 30 minutes.
Every labor is different. Knowing the stages can help you understand what is happening and how much farther there is to go.

🤲 Positions That Help in Labor
  Moving and changing positions can help you cope with labor and may help your baby move down. Try walking, swaying, rocking on a birthing ball, leaning forward over a bed or counter, kneeling on hands and knees, or sitting backward on a chair. A warm shower can bring relief.
Your support person can rub your lower back, press on your hips, or hold you as you sway. If you have an epidural, the nurses can help you change positions in bed. Listen to your body, and try what feels right.

🩺 Your Baby's First Doctor Visit
  Your baby will usually see a doctor within a few days of going home. The doctor will check your baby's weight, feeding, jaundice, and overall health, and answer your questions. Bring your journal, your hospital papers, your diaper count, and your list of questions.
This is the start of many visits in the first year. Write each date and what the doctor said. These notes will help you see how your baby grows and learns.

💙 Dads Can Struggle Too
  Mothers are not the only ones who can feel low after a baby is born. Some fathers feel anxious, sad, or overwhelmed in the weeks and months after birth. Lack of sleep, new responsibilities, and money worries can all play a part.
  Dad, if you feel this way, tell your wife, a friend, your pastor, or your doctor. Asking for help is a sign of strength. A healthy father is a gift to his whole family.

🙏 A Prayer for Labor
Write a short prayer for labor on a card and put it in your bag. It might be as simple as: "Lord, be with me. Give me strength and peace. Keep my baby safe. Help me trust You." Ask your support person to read it to you when labor gets hard.
  You can also pray between tightenings, or ask your support person to pray out loud. Many mothers find that a familiar prayer and a familiar song bring calm when everything else feels new.

💓 Watching Your Baby in Labor
  During labor, your care team will listen to your baby's heartbeat regularly. This may be done with a handheld device from time to time, or with belts around your belly connected to a monitor. The heartbeat tells them how your baby is handling the tightenings.
If the heart rate pattern changes, the team may ask you to change position, give you fluids or oxygen, or take other steps. Ask questions if you want to understand what they are seeing. They are watching your baby's well-being closely, just as you have been with your daily movement counts.

🥤 Eating and Drinking in Labor
  In early labor at home, light snacks and drinks can help keep up your strength, if your doctor agrees: toast, crackers, fruit, broth, juice, or water. Once you are in the hospital, your care team will tell you what you can eat or drink. Many hospitals allow clear fluids during labor, and some allow light food.
Bring snacks for your support person too. Labor can be long, and a hungry, tired support person is less help. After birth, you will probably be very hungry. Plan a favorite meal for after your baby arrives.

🌿 Your First Day After Birth
  In the first hours after birth, your nurse will press on your belly to check that your womb is getting firm, which helps control bleeding. You will have bleeding like a heavy period. The nurse will help you get up to use the bathroom the first time, because you may feel dizzy.
You may feel shaky, emotional, very hungry, or very tired. That is normal. Rest, eat, drink, and let the nurses help you with your baby. Tell your nurse right away if you are soaking a large pad in an hour, passing large clots, or feel faint.

🎵 A Song for the Hospital Room
  Ask your support person to play your weekly songs softly in the hospital room after birth. Familiar music can make a strange place feel like home, for you and for your baby. When visitors come, let them hear the songs too, and teach them the welcome song.
These first hours are the beginning of your baby's life in your family. Let them be filled with the sounds of home.

🧺 The Last Load of Laundry
  In these final days, many mothers feel the urge to finish everything: one more load of laundry, one more meal in the freezer, one more cleaned closet. Do what you can, but do not wear yourself out. Labor takes a lot of energy, and you will want to start it rested.
Choose one small task a day, and then rest. Let the rest go. Your baby will not remember if the closets were clean. Your baby will remember your voice.

🌙 Sleep Before Labor
  Labor can begin at any hour. If you can, rest well in these last days. Go to bed early. Take a nap in the afternoon. If you cannot sleep, rest anyway: lie on your side, close your eyes, and listen to the weekly song.
If labor starts at night and tightenings are mild, try to rest between them for as long as you can. You will be glad you saved your strength.

👨 For Dad: Words of Strength in Labor
  Dad, in labor, your words matter. Simple words of encouragement can help her keep going: "You are doing it." "I am right here." "One at a time." "God is with you." "Our baby is coming."
  Avoid asking a lot of questions during strong tightenings. Instead, watch what helps her and do more of it. Hold her hand, rub her back, offer water, and sing softly if she likes. Your calm presence is one of the best gifts you can give her.

🫶 After the Birth, Hold On
When your baby is finally in your arms, slow down. Count the fingers and toes. Breathe in that newborn smell. Let your baby rest on your chest and hear your heartbeat, the sound your baby has known since the beginning. The paperwork, the phone calls, and the photos can wait a few minutes. These first moments come only once.

🧘 Trusting Your Body
  God designed your body for this. For 39 weeks it has grown, protected, and nourished your baby. In labor, it will open and push and bring your baby into the world. Trust the work God has done in you. Listen to your care team, use the tools you have practiced, and remember that you do not do this alone.

💬 What to Say to Your Newborn
Many parents wonder what to say to a newborn. The answer is simple: say anything, in a loving voice. Tell your baby what you are doing. Tell your baby what you see. Tell your baby that God made them and loves them. Sing the songs your baby knows. Your words, spoken with love, are exactly what your baby needs.

🥗 Body: Caring for the Home This Week
This week, keep easy, energy-giving foods on hand: fruit, toast, yogurt, soup, crackers, and juice. Keep drinking water. Early labor can last many hours, and light snacks and fluids can help, if your doctor agrees.
  Keep up safe food habits right to the end. Cook meats, chicken, eggs, and seafood fully. Rinse produce. Choose pasteurized dairy. Heat deli meats until steaming. Pick low-mercury fish, and avoid shark, swordfish, king mackerel, and tilefish.
  No amount of alcohol is known to be safe while pregnant. Avoid smoking, vaping, and secondhand smoke. Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day. Ask before any medicine, herb, or supplement.

🚨 Signs to Call About Now
Call your doctor or midwife right away if your water breaks, especially if the fluid is green or brown, if your baby is moving much less than usual, or if you have bright red bleeding.
  Call when your tightenings come as often and as long as your doctor told you, or right away for a severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, pain high on the right side of the belly, or a fever.
If you cannot reach your doctor and something seems wrong, go to the hospital.

👨 For Dad: The Day Is Coming
Dad, you have been with her for 39 weeks of songs, prayers, and preparation. The day is coming. Stay close, keep your phone on, and be ready to go.
  In labor, your calm voice, your hand, and your prayers matter more than anything. Help her breathe slowly. Remind her of the weekly song. Speak words of strength.
When your baby is born, sing the welcome song. Then sing the weekly song your child has heard for months. Watch your baby's face as your voice fills the room.

👵 For Grandparents and Siblings
  Big brothers and sisters can practice the welcome song one more time. They can choose one word from the Word List to sing to the baby on the first day home.
  Grandparents can be on call, ready to help. Pray together as a family for a safe labor and a healthy baby.

🎶 One Song, Three Ways: Week 39
Every week has one GUP song, learned three different ways. A good preschool teacher never teaches an important lesson only once. Teach it three ways, and it is remembered.
  Hear it. In the morning, listen once with your eyes closed. Thank God for bringing your baby to full term.
  Hum it. At midday, put on headphones and hum along. Then sing one group of words from your Word List to the tune.
  Write it. In the evening, listen with your Pregnancy Journal open. Read your whole Word List aloud, and circle the words you will sing first after birth.
GUP songs are baby music with a purpose: gentle like lullabies, repeating like nursery rhymes, and full of the phonic songs that become the building blocks of reading.

📓 Your Pregnancy Journal: Week-39 Pages
On your Word List page, circle the first words you will sing after birth.
On a "Full Term" page, write how you feel now that your baby is full term. Write the plan your doctor gave you if labor does not start.
  Keep your "Daily Movement" page going. Add a prayer for labor, for birth, and for the first song you will sing to your baby.

🧭 God's GPS
  You have reached full term. You have done all you can to prepare. Now the last step is God's. He will choose the day, and He will be with you through every moment of labor.
Whatever happens, whether labor is fast or slow, natural or induced, vaginal or cesarean, God directs the steps. Your job now is to trust Him, rest, and be ready to welcome your child.
“The heart of man disposes his way. But it is for the Lord to direct his steps.” (Proverbs 16:9, CPDV)
“Tennessee Ernie Ford was born February 13, 1919. He ended his television shows with a hymn, and his 1956 album of hymns became one of the best-selling gospel records of its time.”

🙏 A Prayer for Week 39
  "Father God, thank You for bringing our baby to full term. Every organ is formed, every reflex is ready, and our baby knows our voices.
  Your faithfulness is new every morning. Give us strength and peace as we wait. When labor comes, be near. When our baby is born, let our first words be words of welcome, and our first song be a song of praise. Let every breath our child ever takes praise You. Direct our steps. In Jesus' name, amen."

❓ Questions Parents Ask
  What does full term mean? Babies born from 39 weeks through 40 weeks and 6 days are full term, the time with the best health outcomes for most babies.
What if I go past my due date? Many first-time mothers do. Your doctor will check on you and your baby and talk with you about induction if labor does not start.
What is an induction? Using medicine or other methods to help labor start. Ask your doctor why they recommend it and what to expect.
Will my baby know our songs? Studies show newborns respond to familiar voices and sounds they heard often before birth. Sing the weekly songs after birth and watch.
  When do I call my doctor right away? Call if your water breaks, for much less movement than usual, bright red bleeding, tightenings as your doctor instructed, a severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling, or a fever.

✅ Your Week-39 Checklist
I took my prenatal vitamin every day. I noticed my baby's movements daily. I asked my doctor about the plan if labor does not start. The bag is in the car.
  I heard, hummed, and wrote this week's one song every day. I sang through my whole Word List. I circled my first words to sing. Dad practiced the welcome song. The family prayed for a safe birth.

🎵 Why We Sing
Every GLAL lesson comes with its own baby music. These phonic songs are made to be sung by Mom, Dad, and the whole family, so your baby learns your real voices. Like the lullabies and nursery rhymes you grew up with, they are simple kids music that a newborn will hear again and again after birth. Sing this week's song today, and let it become the first kids music in your home.

📚 Source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. General pregnancy education only, not medical advice. Always talk with your doctor or midwife.
